survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This policy brief uses PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 international assessment results and PIRLS background questionnaire information (e.g., principals’ reports for schooling time and teachers’ reports for effective teaching time). The analysis is conducted at the country/benchmarking-participant level (e.g., Table 1 trends across countries and Table 2 expected score changes by country), so the brief does not describe student-level complex survey weighting or replicate-weight procedures. Because the paper does not report any specific weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate design methods, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text. For replication with PIRLS microdata, analysts should apply PIRLS sampling weights and plausible-value procedures as specified in the PIRLS technical documentation, but this brief itself presents descriptive/correlational and country-level associations rather than a fully specified weighted microdata model.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent outcomes in this policy brief are country-level average reading achievement scores and country-level changes/associations with schooling time and effective teaching time, rather than student-level plausible-value (PV) outcomes modeled directly in the text. As a result, PV handling is not applicable to the brief’s reported country-level analyses. Missing-data handling is not described because the brief does not provide the underlying microdata processing steps (e.g., case deletion or imputation rules) needed to assess how missing questionnaire or time-use inputs were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 data to examine country-level trends for education systems that participated in both cycles; Table 1 reports trends for the subset of countries/benchmarking participants appearing in both PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 (36 systems listed). Schooling time per year was estimated from principals’ reports in the PIRLS school questionnaire (school days per year and instructional hours per day). For effective teaching time, the brief uses PIRLS 2006 teacher-reported proportions of class time devoted to whole-class instruction or small-group/individual work, excluding administrative and discipline-related time; Table 2 includes 12 of the 36 systems for which this relationship was analyzed.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA policy brief synthesizes PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 evidence on how time in school relates to fourth-grade reading achievement across countries and benchmarking participants. It estimates annual classroom hours from principals’ reports and compares changes in average reading achievement between the two PIRLS cycles (Table 1), finding that increases in total classroom time are not consistently associated with higher reading achievement. It then computes correlations between annual classroom hours and reading achievement using PIRLS 2011 data, reporting small, non-significant correlations across systems (e.g., coefficients ranging from about −0.21 to 0.12). Finally, it uses PIRLS 2006 teacher background data to estimate effective teaching time (instructional activities excluding administrative/discipline time) and reports expected reading score changes for each 10% increase in effective teaching time (Table 2), with a significant positive relationship in 12 systems and negative or non-significant patterns elsewhere. The brief is descriptive/country-level and does not provide a full microdata modeling specification (e.g., weights, PV handling, or missing-data procedures), so causal claims cannot be inferred from the reported associations.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a policy brief that reports country-level descriptive trends and correlations rather than an empirical student-level ML modeling study. As such, it does not specify an ML algorithm set, PV handling, missing-data strategy, or student-level sample sizes, and it does not provide a structured predictive pipeline with model metrics. The extraction therefore leaves ML-related fields empty and focuses on the assessment design and the reported benchmarking results.
